name: Clear cell sarcoma (EWSR1-ATF1, melanoma of soft parts)
aliases: clear cell sarcoma of soft tissue

reference.source: WHO Classification of Tumours of Soft Tissue and Bone
clinicalPearls: A rare soft-tissue sarcoma with melanocytic differentiation, historically called malignant melanoma of soft parts
Typically affects young to middle-aged adults and characteristically involves the deep soft tissue of the distal extremities, especially around the foot, ankle, and tendons or aponeuroses
Often presents as a slowly growing, sometimes painful deep mass attached to tendons or fascia
Expresses melanocytic markers such as S100, SOX10, HMB-45, and Melan-A, closely resembling metastatic melanoma histologically
Distinguished from cutaneous melanoma by a defining EWSR1-ATF1 (or less commonly EWSR1-CREB1) fusion and by the absence of BRAF mutations typical of melanoma
Molecular demonstration of the EWSR1 rearrangement is essential to separate it from metastatic melanoma when morphology and immunohistochemistry overlap
Wide surgical excision is the primary treatment, with radiotherapy for local control; it responds poorly to conventional cytotoxic chemotherapy
Has a marked tendency for regional lymph node involvement as well as distant metastasis, so nodal assessment is important
reference.pathophysiology: Clear cell sarcoma is a translocation-associated malignancy showing melanocytic differentiation, defined by a EWSR1-ATF1 fusion gene (or the less common EWSR1-CREB1 variant). The chimeric fusion protein aberrantly activates the microphthalmia-associated transcription factor (MITF) pathway, driving melanocytic gene expression and accounting for the tumour's pigment-related markers and melanoma-like appearance. Despite this resemblance, it is genetically distinct from cutaneous melanoma, lacking the characteristic melanoma driver mutations, and its defining fusion provides the basis for accurate diagnosis. The tumour's origin from a primitive neural crest-derived cell explains its melanocytic phenotype in a deep soft-tissue location.
additionalDifferentials: Malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour with melanocytic features
Other spindle or epithelioid soft-tissue sarcomas
additionalInvestigations: MRI of the primary site to define deep extent and relation to tendons and fascia
Regional lymph node assessment given the propensity for nodal spread
Biopsy with careful tract planning and immunohistochemistry for melanocytic markers
Molecular testing for EWSR1 rearrangement and, where needed, assessment for BRAF mutation to help exclude melanoma
redFlags: A deep, enlarging soft-tissue mass near tendons of the distal extremity in a young adult
Regional lymphadenopathy accompanying an extremity soft-tissue mass
A mass with melanocytic marker positivity but no cutaneous primary melanoma identified
New respiratory symptoms suggesting pulmonary metastases
reference.prognosis: Clear cell sarcoma carries a guarded prognosis with frequent late recurrence and metastasis to lymph nodes and lung; outcome relates to tumour size, resectability, and nodal status, and its poor response to conventional chemotherapy contributes to the difficulty of controlling advanced disease.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing the tumour as metastatic melanoma on the basis of melanocytic markers alone
Omitting molecular testing for the EWSR1 fusion that distinguishes it from melanoma
Neglecting regional lymph node evaluation despite its notable nodal spread
Relying on conventional chemotherapy, to which the tumour is largely resistant
Poor biopsy planning that complicates limb-sparing surgery
references: WHO Classification of Tumours of Soft Tissue and Bone
Enzinger and Weiss's Soft Tissue Tumors
management: Manage in conjunction with a sarcoma multidisciplinary team, and confirm the EWSR1-ATF1 or EWSR1-CREB1 fusion molecularly before definitive treatment planning to exclude metastatic melanoma
For localized disease, treat with wide local excision of the primary tumor aiming for clear margins
Remove gross regional nodal disease together with resection of the primary tumor given this subtype's tendency for nodal spread
Consider sentinel lymph node biopsy given the tendency toward nodal metastasis, though its clinical utility is debated and not mandatory
Consider adjuvant radiotherapy for local control as a reasonable adjunct within a sarcoma multidisciplinary setting
Assess regional lymph nodes and stage for distant metastases, particularly pulmonary, given the disease's metastatic pattern
Recognize that conventional cytotoxic chemotherapy has limited efficacy in advanced or metastatic disease
Among cytotoxic options, platinum-containing regimens appear to offer the most potential benefit, though responses remain limited overall
Consider antiangiogenic agents (multikinase or VEGF-pathway inhibitors) as an option with reported activity in some cases, based on limited data rather than established standard of care
Favor enrollment in clinical trials or evaluation for targeted or investigational approaches for advanced disease given the poor response to conventional chemotherapy
Refer to a sarcoma specialist center or multidisciplinary team at diagnosis, ideally before biopsy, since biopsy tract planning affects the feasibility of limb-sparing resection
Refer for molecular pathology confirmation of the EWSR1 rearrangement when morphology and immunohistochemistry (S100, HMB-45, melan-A) raise the differential of metastatic melanoma
Refer to medical oncology for consideration of platinum-based systemic therapy or clinical trial enrollment in metastatic or unresectable disease
Continue long-term surveillance imaging of the primary site, regional nodal basin, and chest given the potential for late recurrence and distant metastasis
